summary: Describes CCNinfo, an experimental tool for Content-Centric Networks that discovers routing path information per name prefix, round-trip time between forwarder and consumer, and the state of in-network caches. It is meant to help understand and debug testbeds and other experimental CCN deployments.

plainLanguage.summary: Like a detective for a network where you ask for things by name instead of by address. It finds which way the request went, how long it took, and which stops had a saved copy.

subtitle: A tool to trace routing paths and inspect cache state in name-based networks.

tldr.problem: In Content-Centric Networks where routers forward by content name rather than address, operators need tools to understand routing paths and inspect the state of in-network caches, much as IP traceroute reveals paths in IP networks.
tldr.mechanism: CCNinfo sends Request messages upstream toward content sources. Each router along the path adds information to the message, and the content forwarder replies, sending back routing path information, round-trip time, and details of cached copies.
tldr.outcome: Operators gain visibility into experimental CCN deployments, enabling troubleshooting and performance analysis. The tool supports multipath discovery and policy-based hiding of sensitive information.

facts.label: Cache metrics
facts.value: Object size, count, access count, first and last sequence numbers, lifetime

today: RFC 9344 is an Experimental protocol published in February 2023. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and remains a tool for research and experimental CCN testbeds rather than a production protocol.

sections.title: Discovering Paths and Caches in Name-Based Networks
sections.content:
Content-Centric Networks (CCNs) let applications request content by name rather than by IP address. Routers forward named content requests, and in-network caches store frequently accessed copies. While this architecture is powerful for application developers, operators and researchers need tools to understand how content is being routed and where it is cached.

CCNinfo provides this visibility. Like the traceroute tool in IP networks, it traces the path a request follows toward a content source. Unlike traceroute, CCNinfo discovers which routers along the path hold cached copies, measures the round-trip time from the consumer to each cache or source, and retrieves cache statistics such as the number of cached objects and their sizes. CCNinfo embeds itself directly in forwarders and works with the CCN Forwarding daemon.

The tool is designed for experimental testbeds and research deployments where operators need detailed instrumentation to measure protocol performance and troubleshoot network conditions. It supports policy-based information provisioning, allowing operators to hide sensitive details while still enabling the tracing and discovery capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: CCNinfo is a detective tool for name-based networks. You tell it a content name, and it traces backward toward the source, noting which routers it passes and how long the trip takes. Along the way, it learns which routers have a saved copy on hand.

sections.title: Request and Reply Messages
sections.content:
CCNinfo defines two message types: Request and Reply, encoded in the CCNx TLV (Type-Length-Value) binary format. A CCNinfo user initiates a Request message with a content name prefix or exact name. Each Request includes a fixed header with a hop limit (like TTL in IP), a Request header block that carries the request ID and flags indicating what to discover, and a Report block that the user fills with its own information.

As the Request travels upstream toward the source, each router along the path adds its own Report block to the message, recording its node identifier and the time the Request arrived. The message may travel through multiple upstream routers (for multipath discovery) if the user sets the full-discovery flag.

When the Request reaches a router that has the content cached, or when it reaches the first-hop router connected to the publisher, that router converts the Request into a Reply message and sends it back toward the consumer. The Reply message carries all the Report blocks from the path, plus a Reply block with details of the cache state: the total size of cached objects, the count of cached objects, the number of times those objects were requested, and their lifetime and expiration times.
sections.plainLanguage: A Request message is like a letter with a return address. Each router on the path writes its name and the time it arrived on the envelope. When the message reaches a cache or the source, it becomes a Reply and travels back, collecting signatures from each hop.

sections.title: How Routers Handle Requests
sections.content:
When a router receives a CCNinfo Request, it first checks whether the message should be forwarded at all: does it have a route for the requested name prefix? Is the request signed and valid if the router enforces access control? It also checks the hop limit and skip-hop count (which lets users skip the first N routers without tracing them).

The router then examines the request flags to determine what kind of discovery is being requested. For routing path discovery, the router simply adds its Report block and forwards the Request upstream if it does not hold the content. For cache information discovery, the router first checks its own cache. If it holds the content, it replies immediately with cache statistics. If not, it forwards the Request upstream. The full-discovery flag tells the router to forward the Request to all possible upstream routers simultaneously, so the user can trace all paths.

Routers forward replies back along the path they recorded in the Pending Interest Table (PIT), similar to the way they forward content in normal Interest-Data exchanges. If multiple replies arrive from different paths, the user program receives all of them and can analyze the different routing paths and cache locations.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router acts like a mail clerk. If the content is in the local cache, the router writes a reply immediately. Otherwise, it notes the request time on the envelope and passes it upstream. Replies travel back down the path they came from.

sections.title: Protecting Against Information Leakage
sections.content:
CCNinfo exposes detailed information about network topology, cache state, and forwarding paths. A router operator might not want to reveal which content is cached, or which routers serve certain name prefixes. To address this, CCNinfo implements policy-based information provisioning: routers can filter or hide sensitive information from certain users or networks.

The protocol supports validation of Request messages using cryptographic signatures, so a router can verify that a request comes from an authorized user before revealing information. Routers can also limit the rate at which they process requests to prevent CCNinfo from being used as a denial-of-service tool. Routers may require full-discovery requests to carry a signature, since multipath tracing reveals more topology than regular discovery.

CCNinfo also includes a mechanism to verify that replies come from valid adjacent neighbors, so routers can reject spoofed or man-in-the-middle replies. Operators can administratively disable CCNinfo or restrict it to specific networks, and they can configure CCNinfo reply timeouts to tune the trade-off between gathering complete path information and keeping request overhead low.
sections.plainLanguage: CCNinfo can reveal secrets about the network, so routers can decide what to hide. They can ask you to prove who you are, ignore requests that come too fast, and ignore fake replies from nodes that should not be on the path.

sections.title: What You Can Learn from CCNinfo
sections.content:
CCNinfo replies provide several kinds of useful data. Hop count and round-trip time (RTT): by examining the Report blocks and Reply block in a single reply, you can see how many hops separate you from the content forwarder and measure the RTT. If multiple replies arrive, you can compare the RTT of different paths. Cache location: if one reply comes from a caching router and another from the first-hop router of the publisher, you know there is a cache on the path and where it is.

Cache popularity and hit rate: the Reply block includes the number of times content was requested (received Interests), so you can compute which cached objects are frequently accessed. If you send multiple CCNinfo requests over time, you can estimate the cache hit probability for a name prefix. Path diversity: using the full-discovery flag, you can map all possible forwarding paths and find which ones yield cached content versus which paths reach the publisher.

The RFC includes a simple analysis tool interface (a ccninfo command) that a user can invoke to send requests and display the results. Developers can interpret the cache timing information to analyze Content Object lifetimes, detect cache eviction patterns, and understand whether content is being served from a nearby cache or from the original publisher.
sections.plainLanguage: From the replies, you learn how far away the content is, which routers have copies on hand, how popular different cached items are, and whether there are multiple ways to reach the source.
